en: Taal Volcano in Batangas emits sulfur dioxide gas that can trigger severe asthma attacks for residents living in downwind areas.
Mount Pulag in Benguet drops to near-freezing temperatures at dawn, requiring hikers to wear thick jackets to prevent hypothermia.
The highly polluted Pasig River in Manila contains dangerous bacteria, so children must avoid wading in its water to prevent leptospirosis.
Coastal towns near the Philippine Trench in Eastern Samar experience strong earthquake tremors, so residents must immediately run to higher ground to avoid tsunamis.
Because the Philippines lies directly on the equator, students must apply sunscreen daily to prevent severe sunburns and heatstroke.
Stagnant rainwater collected in empty coconut shells around rural homes in Davao breeds mosquitoes that transmit the deadly dengue virus.
Mayon Volcano in Albay has a strict six-kilometer Permanent Danger Zone to protect locals from sudden, deadly pyroclastic flows during eruptions.
The dense mangrove forests along the coast of Olango Island in Cebu act as natural barriers that protect villages from destructive typhoon storm surges.
The Angat Dam in Bulacan supplies most of Metro Manila's drinking water, meaning residents must fix leaky faucets to prevent water shortages.
The San Bernardino Strait between Luzon and Samar has strong tidal currents, so passengers must wear life jackets during rough ferry rides.
Baguio City receives heavy monsoon rains that saturate the Cordillera mountains, so residents must evacuate immediately if they hear rumbling sounds indicating a landslide.
The rich volcanic soil near Mount Kanlaon in Negros Occidental yields great crops, but farmers must evacuate immediately when the volcano emits loud explosion sounds.
